evidence.sourceText: When Jupiter made himself ruler of the world, he imprisoned some of the warring giants under Mount Etna in Sicily, much to the disgust of Pluto, who was always fearing that when the giants got restless and turned over and over underground (thus causing earthquakes), they would some day make such a large crack in the earth that daylight would be let into Hades.

In a moment Pluto had seized her in his strong arms; and, trampling all her violets under his ruthless feet, he sprang into the chariot and urged his horses to their full speed, hoping to reach Hades before the maiden's cries brought Ceres to the rescue.
Proserpina alone stood still, and stared, frightened and wondering, at the grim figure confronting her, while the flowers she had gathered dropped from her trembling hands.

When Ceres[37] came that evening into the vale of Enna and found that her daughter was not playing as usual with the other maidens, she questioned them, and learned their tearful story of the chariot with its four black horses and terrible driver.

Mercury was sent to lead Proserpina out of Hades; but when he reached there, he found that Pluto had already given his wife some pomegranate seeds, hoping that she would thereby stay forever in his keeping.

narrative.synopsis: Pluto seizes Proserpina in Sicily and carries her into Hades. Ceres searches for her daughter and neglects the earth until famine moves Jupiter to arrange a compromise that divides Proserpina's time between her mother and Pluto.
narrative.openingSituation: Jupiter has imprisoned the giants under Mount Etna, and Pluto leaves Hades to inspect the earth for cracks.
narrative.centralConflict: Pluto abducts Proserpina by force, and Ceres cannot find her daughter.
narrative.resolution: Jupiter intervenes during the famine and compromises with Pluto after Proserpina has eaten pomegranate seeds.
narrative.outcome: Proserpina spends part of her time with Ceres and part with Pluto, and Ceres restores the earth when Proserpina returns.
